ops.title: fleet-build could not build a consumer whose module is not at its checkout root, so cc-skills was never gated
ops.body:
Found and fixed 2026-08-29 while closing out the daemonkit v0.23.0 state-root migration. Fixed in `af2dbf5`.

## The gap

`cc-skills` is a genuine daemonkit consumer — module `github.com/yasyf/cc-skills/plugins/codex`, shipping the `codex-ask` Homebrew cask — and the fleet-build gate had **never built it**. It was absent from `.github/workflows/fleet-build.yml`'s matrix and from `ci/fleet-refs.txt`.

That absence was **structural, not an oversight**. `checkout_of` resolved a module to `$src_dir/${module##*/}` — the module *basename* — so `cc-skills`' module resolved to `$src_dir/codex`, a directory that does not exist. Every `go.mod` read (`go_directive`, `fleet_requires`, `module_of`, `pinned_daemonkit`, `snapshot_manifest`, `restore_manifest`) and the build's own `cd "$source_dir"` all assumed the module sat at the checkout root. Adding a matrix line would not have worked; the script could not express the consumer.

## Why it mattered

The gate's stated purpose is that "a breaking surface change goes red BEFORE a release exists", and `ci/fleet-refs.txt` refuses a file that leaves any consumer undeclared, "because an omitted leg silently builds a branch nobody chose". Both guarantees were sound — and both were scoped to a consumer set that could not include cc-skills.

The visible consequence: cc-skills sat on **daemonkit v0.21.4** while all thirteen other consumers moved to v0.22.0 and then v0.23.0. It missed *both* state-root moves. Nothing reported it, because the only mechanism that would have was the gate that structurally excluded it. See [[a-daemonkit-consumer-migrates-when-it-ships-not-when-its-main-is-bumped]] for why an unbuilt consumer also stays unmigrated on every host.

## The grammar, and why not the obvious one

`ci/fleet-refs.txt` is now `<repo>[:<module-dir>] <ref> [goos[,goos]...]`, e.g. `cc-skills:plugins/codex  main`.

A bare fourth column was rejected: column three (the GOOS set) is optional, so a three-field line is ambiguous between `<repo> <ref> <goos>` and `<repo> <ref> <module-dir>`, and `check_refs` could not distinguish malformed from well-formed. A mandatory third column defaulting to `.` would rewrite all thirteen existing lines for one consumer and kill the optional-GOOS shape the header documents.

The colon form wins on a real property rather than taste: `<repo>:<module-dir>` **is exactly the module path minus the `github.com/<owner>/` prefix**, so the mapping is derivable in both directions instead of guessed. `checkout_of` now resolves by prefix strip and still requires the `go.mod` found there to declare that exact module — which reaches *into* the subdirectory rather than stopping at the repository, a strictly stronger identity check than the basename strip it replaces. `:` cannot appear in a GitHub repo name or a GOOS value, and everything that addresses a leg by name (`--only`, `--ref`, `--cone`, a cone peer, `matrix.repo`, `actions/checkout`'s `path`) still takes the bare repo, so the workflow needed only a matrix entry and a widened `cache-dependency-path` glob.

## What the adversarial review then found — the more important half

Two independent review passes (finder and refuter) over the change surfaced **five confirmed defects**, three of them false greens in a release gate. They are worth recording because most were **pre-existing**, not regressions from this change:

1. **Data loss via relative `FLEET_SRC`.** `snapshot_manifest` embedded the uncanonicalized checkout path under `$work/orig`, so `FLEET_SRC=../../../..` normalized the backup target *outside* `$work` and overwrote an unrelated file — which the `EXIT` trap, scoped to `fleet-build.*`, then left behind. This violated the script's own explicit promise to leave every overlaid checkout byte-identical.
2. **A zero-package module reported PASS**, because `go build ./...` exits 0 when `./...` matches nothing. A consumer that lost all its Go files, or excluded them under a build tag, would have reported `1/1 built`.
3. **A comma-only GOOS set ran no build at all** and kept `verdict=PASS` — the loop over `${goos_set//,/ }` simply had zero iterations.
4. `cc-skills:.` passed validation and silently selected the root module, skipping the nested one.
5. `module_dir`/`repo_of` emitted data with `echo`, so a module dir of `-n` was consumed as an option.

**The lesson worth carrying:** a gate's own correctness is not covered by the gate. Three of these five made the script report success while measuring nothing, and none would ever have gone red to announce itself. A release gate earns an adversarial pass of its own — and specifically a **mutation check**: prove the leg goes red when the thing it guards actually breaks, not merely that it goes green when everything is fine.

## The verification shape that settled it

Per finding, a green→red→green bracket against the *reviewed* code — rebuilt so the reviewers' cited line numbers land exactly, so the "before" column is the reviewed script rather than an approximation.

For the gate as a whole: renaming `daemonkit.Stable` makes the cc-skills leg FAIL with `./daemon_runtime.go:17:28: undefined: daemonkit.Stable` against cc-skills' *own* source file — proving the leg compiles the consumer rather than no-opping, and ruling out a daemonkit self-build failure — and restoring it makes the leg PASS.

For regression safety: full fleet 14/14, against a **retained** baseline worktree running the unmodified `origin/main` script at 13/13, whose only textual difference is the leg count. Every shared leg's verdict, `*` mark, ref, pin, path, described revision and cone list is byte-identical. The baseline worktree is still on disk at `~/.claude/worktrees/daemonkit/gate-baseline`, so parity is re-runnable rather than asserted — the reviewer's specific objection to the first attempt, which had claimed parity from an edited excerpt after deleting the baseline.
